Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.

sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

inspect:2610.11730.question: In the LLaMA compression experiments, locate the results tables comparing spectral weight decay with standard weight decay, Cuttlefish, and Prehab at matched validation loss: report each compression ratio and inference speedup. In the 60% label-noise experiments, locate the clean-test accuracy tables, seed counts, and matching protocol.

passages.text: To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

The main experiments use Adam-family optimizers. Conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay is routinely used across optimizer families, so we also examine whether spectral weight decay transfers beyond Adam. Its decoupled correction can be applied to the candidate weights produced by any optimizer, but the resulting loss and rank dynamics depend on the optimizer. Figure 6 : Optimizer-dependent loss and rank dynamics. The top row shows validation loss, and the bottom row shows mean effective rank. The columns compare ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with coefficient 0.1 0.1 across optimizers, spectral regularization with Muon, and spectral regularization with Lion. Colors match between the loss and rank panels. Figure 6 (a,d) compares optimizers with the same ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay coefficient of 0.1 0.1 . Muon [ Jordan et al., 2024 ] and SOAP [ Vyas et al., 2024 ] produce higher effective ranks than the other optimizers, whose final ranks cluster in a narrow range. This suggests that their optimization dynamics may oppose the spectral concentration encouraged by spectral weight decay. The Muon sweep in Figure 6 (b,e) shows that substantial rank reduction comes with a steep validation-loss increase, limiting the practical appeal of this combination. By contrast, Lion exhibits a more favorable trade-off between loss and rank in Figure 6 (c,f), qualitatively similar to Adam.

The required regularization scale also varies across optimizers. A mean effective rank of about 300 300 requires λ = 0.8 \lambda=0.8 for Adam, λ = 0.4 \lambda=0.4 for Muon, and λ = 4 \lambda=4 for Lion. Although the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} baselines use a common coefficient, spectral weight decay requires optimizer-specific calibration for the desired rank and validation-loss budget. The strong training results reported for Muon motivate adapting the techniques studied here to Muon and related matrix-aware optimizers. Understanding how to combine their optimization benefits with effective spectral regularization remains a direction for future work.

We introduced spectral weight decay by replacing the squared Frobenius penalty of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with the nuclear norm. Its decoupled post-step correction shrinks the spectrum of the updated weights additively, with a stronger relative effect on smaller singular values. The connection to approximate proximal descent supports this choice of update order. Our analysis also shows that pre- and post-step spectral updates can differ more substantially than their ℓ 2 \ell_{2} counterparts near rank deficiency. Across 124 124 M to 500 500 M LLaMA models trained with Adam-family optimizers, the resulting low-effective-rank structure improves post-training compression under matched validation-loss budgets. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, we obtain 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. The benefits extend beyond compression. Under fixed-horizon training with noisy labels, spectral regularization reduces memorization and improves clean-test accuracy on image and text classification tasks. These observations are consistent with the view that concentrating the weight spectrum limits the capacity available to fit corrupted labels. The benefits depend on when and how spectral regularization is applied. Short fine-tuning from a conventional-weight-decay checkpoint incurs a larger loss penalty for rank reduction than regularization during pretraining. Optimizer choice also matters: Adam and Lion exhibit a favorable trade-off between loss and rank, whereas the Muon runs show a steeper loss increase as rank decreases. Adapting spectral regularization to matrix-aware optimizers and reducing the cost of preparing existing checkpoints for low-rank compression remain open problems.

BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

passages.text: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top- r r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r × r r\times r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%. Our code is available at https://github.com/LiqunMa/ResQAdam .

From-scratch QAT. We consider QuEST ( Panferov et al., 2025 ) and CAGE ( Tabesh et al., 2025 ) , which represent two recent low-precision training frameworks with distinct gradient-estimation and optimization strategies. We pretrain Llama-style models at the 200M and 430M scales under W2A2, W2A16, and W4A4 settings. QAT fine-tuning. We use Basic QAT (end-to-end next-token loss with LSQ scales on 2B RedPajama tokens), LLM-QAT ( Liu et al., 2024 ) (data-free distillation), and the Block-AP stage of EfficientQAT ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , on Llama 3.2-1B, Qwen3 4B-Base and Llama 2-7B under multiple quantization configurations.. State Size reports average optimizer state size for each optimizer during the training, computed only over non-embedding and non-LM-head parameters.

Optimization Trajectory and Convergence Alignment. As illustrated in Figure 2 , ResQAdam closely tracks the training-loss trajectory of the dense AdamW baseline. Across all evaluated bit-width configurations and both frameworks, the training loss curves of ResQAdam closely overlap with the baseline from initialization through to the final iterations. The zoomed-in callouts at the end of the training horizons further highlight that ResQAdam maintains stable convergence without divergence. This confirms that our geometry-decoupled and space-specific update strategies sufficiently capture the quantization errors to stabilize the low-bit pretraining process. Curves for the 200M model are in Appendix B . Language Modeling Quality. Table 1 reports the final validation perplexity across model scales and quantization settings. For both QuEST and CAGE, ResQAdam achieves perplexities close to full-state AdamW, with several cases where ResQAdam is slightly better. These results show that ResQAdam largely preserves AdamW-level language modeling quality in from-scratch QAT while substantially reducing optimizer-state memory.

Total peak memory is defined as the maximum GPU memory consumed during training, encompassing weights, activations, gradients, and optimizer states. All experiments utilize the Basic QAT framework with a W4A4G128 quantization configuration and a context length of 4096. Training is conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. The micro-batch size is set to 1 with 128 gradient accumulation steps. ResQAdam uses a uniform projection rank of r = 64 r=64 . The reported optimizer-state memory strictly accounts for the transformer backbone and excludes the embedding and language modeling head layers.

As detailed in Table 3 , ResQAdam consistently reduces the optimizer state footprint by over 71% across 3 different LLMs. This efficiency directly translates to a 15.3% to 19.5% reduction in total peak memory. This substantial memory reduction incurs minimal computational overhead. The training throughput decreases by less than 2% compared to standard AdamW in all evaluated cases. These results show that our amortized update strategy substantially alleviates the optimizer-state memory bottleneck of QAT while maintaining competitive training throughput.

inspect:2610.23571.question: For the 1B LLaMA-style FineWeb experiment, what are the matched Muon baselines, training and MLP channel-pruning budgets, validation-loss or downstream-quality results, and measured training overhead for BMuon?

passages.text: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon’s optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon’s spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning. Code: https://github.com/RidaAssalouh/BMuon † † shortheadings: BMuon / Assalouh et al.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

To summarize, our main contributions are: • We introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which incorporates a single global hidden-channel budget into Muon’s spectral update geometry, while coupling the matrix slices that define each MLP channel. • We characterize the induced norm family Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} and its relation to Muon and structured sparse geometries in Section 2 . In the linear factorization setting of Section 3 , we show that for a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost is also attained by redundant-width factorizations. • We derive a practical minorization–maximization surrogate for the global allocation problem, yielding a tractable allocation update in Section 4 . • In Section 5 , we show across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model that BMuon improves structured MLP-channel compressibility relative to Muon. In the vision experiments, the learned allocations also provide effective pruning scores and identify non-uniform MLP architectures that outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Our LLaMA/FineWeb experiments are based on the LLaMA-1B setup of Muon+ ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) 1 1 1 https://github.com/K1seki221/MuonPlus . We adopt its architecture and training recipe, reducing only the number of Transformer blocks from 24 24 to 17 17 to obtain a 986,746,880 986{,}746{,}880 -parameter model; all other architectural hyperparameters are unchanged. The Muon+ codebase builds on Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and the modded-nanogpt training framework 2 2 2 https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt . Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon’s optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon’s spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning. Code: https://github.com/RidaAssalouh/BMuon † † shortheadings: BMuon / Assalouh et al.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

To summarize, our main contributions are: • We introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which incorporates a single global hidden-channel budget into Muon’s spectral update geometry, while coupling the matrix slices that define each MLP channel. • We characterize the induced norm family Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} and its relation to Muon and structured sparse geometries in Section 2 . In the linear factorization setting of Section 3 , we show that for a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost is also attained by redundant-width factorizations. • We derive a practical minorization–maximization surrogate for the global allocation problem, yielding a tractable allocation update in Section 4 . • In Section 5 , we show across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model that BMuon improves structured MLP-channel compressibility relative to Muon. In the vision experiments, the learned allocations also provide effective pruning scores and identify non-uniform MLP architectures that outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

Each hyperparameter either follows the recommendation of the original paper or is selected by grid search. For each model and optimizer, we select the hyperparameter configuration that achieves the highest average accuracy across the seven downstream benchmarks, with the chosen values summarized in Table 7 . We report the memory cost of all methods in Table 6 , measured with torch.compile disabled. As shown in Table 8 , PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among all memory-efficient methods across all model scales. Table 9: Accuracy (%) on the IFEval (instruction-following) benchmark. Bold and underlined values indicate the best and second-best results among memory-efficient methods, respectively.

In this section, we provide the omitted details of the LLM supervised finetuning (SFT) experiments. For the instruction-following task, we train on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU and adopt a device micro-batch size of 16 16 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for Muon, GaLore, GoLore, GUM, and PMRC, and a device micro-batch size of 8 8 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is 128 128 in both cases. For the mathematical reasoning task, we train on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs and adopt a device micro-batch size of 4 4 with 8 8 gradient accumulation steps for the same methods and a device micro-batch size of 2 2 with 16 16 gradient accumulation steps for AdamW, so that the global batch size is again 128 128 . For AdamW-based methods, we use the standard coefficients β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 and β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 . For Muon-based methods, the momentum coefficient is set to 1 − β = 0.95 1-\beta=0.95 with Nesterov momentum enabled. The matrix sign is approximated using 5 5 Newton–Schulz iterations, while one-dimensional parameters and embedding layers are optimized with AdamW.

Hyperparameter Tuning. For each model and optimization method we select the learning rate by a grid search over { 1 × 10 − 5 , 2 × 10 − 5 , 4 × 10 − 5 , 8 × 10 − 5 } \{1\times 10^{-5},2\times 10^{-5},4\times 10^{-5},8\times 10^{-5}\} for the instruction-following task and { 8 × 10 − 6 , 1 × 10 − 5 , 3 × 10 − 5 , 5 × 10 − 5 , 7 × 10 − 5 } \{8\times 10^{-6},1\times 10^{-5},3\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-5},7\times 10^{-5}\} for the mathematical-reasoning task. PMRC uses a residual cap at a ratio of 4 4 and we grid search γ ∈ { 2000 , 4000 , 8000 , 16000 } \gamma\in\{2000,4000,8000,16000\} . We select the parameters that achieve the highest accuracy on benchmarks. Additional results. We present the prompt-level and instruction-level strict accuracy on the IFEval benchmark in Table 9 . For completeness, we include the results of GUM with rank r = 256 r=256 , in addition to the memory-matched setting with r = 128 r=128 used in the main experiments. passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Qwen3 Pretraining Tasks. We compare Adam, Muon, and ORCA on Qwen3-style architecture. Within each model scale, all methods share the same common hyperparameters. The Qwen3 0.6B curves cover 50k optimizer steps (about 105B tokens), and the Qwen3 160M curves cover 25k optimizer steps (about 26B tokens). In both Qwen settings, both sets of loss curves show the same ordering: ORCA may fall temporarily behind Muon early in training, then crosses over and holds the advantage at the end of the observed interval. The validation-loss improvement of ORCA is therefore not confined to LLaMA, but also reproduces on the Qwen3 architecture. Larger Scale Fine-grained MoE Pretrining. We observed router perturbations under a fixed global release point, so we release the orthogonal constraint layerwise: at 20 % 20\% of training in the first layer and at 60 % 60\% in the last layer, with release times linearly interpolated across layers. We use top- 4 4 routing with 64 64 experts in the MoE 0.8 0.8 B model ( 0.24 0.24 B active parameters) and 64 64 experts in the MoE 8 8 B model ( 1 1 B active parameters) ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

Early orthogonal shaping also benefits other base optimizers. We apply the same soft orthogonal shaping step ( 3.3 ) to Adam and SOAP on LLaMA 130M ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) . Shaping is active only during the first 25 % 25\% of training; the base optimizer then continues alone. For both optimizers, shaping temporarily raises validation loss while active, but the shaped runs overtake their baselines after its removal and finish lower. At 50k steps, it reduces Adam’s loss from 2.8824 2.8824 to 2.8435 2.8435 and SOAP’s from 2.8640 2.8640 to 2.8271 2.8271 , gains of 0.0389 0.0389 and 0.0369 0.0369 , respectively. These results show that the benefits of early orthogonal shaping extend beyond Muon to other base optimizers. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} . This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation ( B , A ) ∼ ( B ​ G − 1 , A ​ G ⊤ ) (B,A)\sim(BG^{-1},AG^{\top}) for any invertible matrix G G because B ​ A ⊤ = B ​ G − 1 ​ ( A ​ G ⊤ ) ⊤ BA^{\top}=BG^{-1}(AG^{\top})^{\top} and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices ( B ​ G − 1 , A ​ G ⊤ ) (BG^{-1},AG^{\top}) for all G G are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. We theoretically show that LoRA with our preconditioning induced by this metric satisfies the following two properties at each iteration: (i) The weight update follows the direction closest to the gradient of full fine-tuning within the subspace of first-order weight changes allowed by the LoRA parameterization. (ii) The updated weight matrix is closer in Frobenius norm to that of full fine-tuning than the updated weight matrices of LoRA with conventional preconditioning and without preconditioning. These theoretical insights suggest that our preconditioning makes LoRA better approximate full fine-tuning, thereby

Experiments show the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning for LoRA on fine-tuning tasks with language and vision domains.

To validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning 5 for LoRA, we conducted LoRA fine-tuning experiments on natural language generation, image classification, and commonsense reasoning tasks, following the existing LoRA studies [ 21 , 63 , 56 , 41 , 26 ] . All experiments were performed in PyTorch [ 42 ] on a single H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM. We downloaded the pre-trained models using Hugging Face Transformers library [ 57 ] .

Following [ 26 , 41 , 16 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the LLaMA2-7B [ 52 ] on the commonsense reasoning benchmark, which assesses the reasoning capabilities of the fine-tuned model across the eight datasets, such as BoolQ [ 8 ] , PIQA [ 5 ] , SIQA [ 48 ] , HellaS [ 62 ] , WinoG [ 47 ] , ARC-e [ 9 ] , ARC-c [ 9 ] , and OBQA [ 35 ] . In these datasets, we measured the top-1 test accuracy. For fair comparison, we first split a combined dataset of all train sets, i.e., Commonsense170K, into the train and validation sets, tuned the learning rate on the validation set, and then evaluated the fine-tuned model on the test set in each dataset. In this experiment, we tested the Adam methods with preconditioning. We tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for each method on the validation set, similar to Sec. 7.3 . For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query, key, and value projections of the attention layers and the up and down projections of the feed-forward layers. We also fixed the rank to r = 32 r=32 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 64 64 , the batch size to 16 16 , the weight decay to zero, the dropout to 0.05 0.05 , and the train epoch to 3 3 with a linear learning-rate schedule. Table 3 shows the results. We observed that our AdamW method achieves either the highest or second-highest top-1 test accuracy across datasets, leading to the highest average. These results validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning for LoRA on the commonsense reasoning task.

In this paper, we proposed a Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. This metric induces new preconditioning, and we theoretically showed that this preconditioning makes LoRA better approximates full fine-tuning compared with the conventional preconditioning and no preconditioning. Diverse experiments showed the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning in the language and vision domains. This paper is the first to explore the possibility of tailoring a Riemannian metric to LoRA, paving the way for future followers.

Following [ 21 , 63 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the GPT-2 medium model [ 45 ] on E2E natural language generation challenge task [ 38 ] , which assesses the fine-tuned model’s ability to generate fluent and semantically accurate sentences from meaning representations. We followed the same experimental setup as in [ 63 ] , except that we tuned the learning rate over { 0.02 , 0.04 , … , 0.30 } \{0.02,0.04,\dots,0.30\} for SGD and { 0.0002 , 0.0004 , … , 0.0030 } \{0.0002,0.0004,\dots,0.0030\} for AdamW methods on the validation set. For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query and value matrices of the attention layers in the GPT-2 model. We also fixed the rank to r = 4 r=4 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 32 32 , the batch size to 8 8 , the dropout to 0.1 0.1 , and the train epoch to 5 5 with a linear learning-rate schedule. We set the weight decay to 0.01 0.01 for the SGD and AdamW methods. We evaluated all methods by five metrics, BLEU [ 40 ] , NIST [ 12 ] , METEOR [ 3 ] , ROUGE-L [ 27 ] , and CIDEr [ 53 ] , on the test set. passages.text: Figure 2 : MoE pretraining at the same token budget. Two-block Monarch–Muon reaches the reported final validation loss of dense AdamW with fewer active and total parameters. Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer. We compare AdamW and Muon with two and four blocks, using the same token budget and training schedule within each architecture. Dense AdamW, dense Muon, and GaLore provide reference losses for the dense quality model. The MoE comparison retains the same routing architecture and changes only the selected projections and their optimizer. Monarch–Muon achieves lower final validation loss than Monarch–AdamW in all four structured comparisons (Table 1 ). The two-block MoE reaches the reported loss of dense AdamW with 15% fewer active parameters and 25.4% fewer total parameters (767M versus 1.029B). Figure 2 places this endpoint in the training trajectory. Thus, matrix-aware updates remain useful when the optimizer acts on structured factors rather than dense weights. Increasing the block count further reduces storage, with a higher final loss under both optimizers. Dense Muon gives the lowest loss in each architecture, defining the quality reference for this representation tradeoff. The learned spectra provide a complementary view of the optimizer effect. At the same block count, Monarch–Muon retains a heavier singular-value tail than Monarch–AdamW in the gate and up projections (Figure 3 ). Similar patterns appear in additional layers and components (Appendix B ). Thus, the change in update geometry reaches the represented matrices, even though orthogonalization is local to their factors.

inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results for GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC? Which predictions are tested empirically on neural networks or language models, against which optimizer baselines, and what limitations are stated?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

passages.section: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 .
passages.text: Fig. 2 compares quantities measured from the trajectories with the theoretical predictions. For birth, GD retains exponent p p , ideal Muon follows q q , instantaneous Adam interpolates between the Euclidean and normalized regimes, cumulative Shampoo moves from p p toward its history-adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , and undamped K-FAC removes the singular-magnitude dependence with α b = 0 \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}=0 . The decay curves distinguish finite extinction under ideal Muon, exponential decay under undamped K-FAC, and the polynomial tails of GD and cumulative Shampoo. The saturation experiment further reveals optimizer-dependent mode ordering: GD and Adam converge faster for larger targets; undamped K-FAC is approximately target independent while Muon shows dependence; history-dominated Shampoo reverses the GD ordering. Thus the optimizers change relative spectral progress rather than merely rescaling a common trajectory. Figure 2: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 at depth L = 4 L=4 . (a) The birth exponent α b \alpha_{\mathrm{b}} separates Euclidean, normalized, history adapted, and curvature corrected dynamics. (b) The decay exponent α d \alpha_{\mathrm{d}} distinguishes finite extinction of Muon ( α d = q < 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{d}}\!=\!q\!<\!1 ) from the other optimizers. (c) The saturation coefficient β \beta reveals target dependent mode ordering. (a) Adam ϵ \epsilon controls the regime (b) Two phases of Shampoo (c) K-FAC λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\!>\!0 restores barrier Figure 3: Optimizer state parameters control the local birth regime. Adam’s stability parameter ϵ \epsilon shifts the GD-to-SignGD crossover; Shampoo damping delays the transition from p p to p − 1 p-1 ; and K-FAC damping restores the GD exponent below its curvature threshold.

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Analysis of Muon in matrix factorization.
passages.text: Kang et al. (2026) analyze spectral gradient flow in a simplified LoRA factorization setting, proving approximately equal spectral growth rates and convergence results under stated conditions. Dragutinović and Ranganath (2026) derive dynamics for simplified Muon in deep linear networks and linear attention and investigate how avoiding slow sequential learning changes simplicity bias. Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. They also study alignment in simplified settings. These results already establish much of the ideal polar growth baseline. Our treatment places it alongside memory dependent adaptive flows and damped curvature flows, with separate statements for birth, saturation, and zero target decay. Parviz et al. inspect:2610.04249.text:
Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Fig. 2 compares quantities measured from the trajectories with the theoretical predictions. For birth, GD retains exponent p p , ideal Muon follows q q , instantaneous Adam interpolates between the Euclidean and normalized regimes, cumulative Shampoo moves from p p toward its history-adapted exponent p − 1 p-1 , and undamped K-FAC removes the singular-magnitude dependence with α b = 0 \alpha_{\mathrm{b}}=0 . The decay curves distinguish finite extinction under ideal Muon, exponential decay under undamped K-FAC, and the polynomial tails of GD and cumulative Shampoo. The saturation experiment further reveals optimizer-dependent mode ordering: GD and Adam converge faster for larger targets; undamped K-FAC is approximately target independent while Muon shows dependence; history-dominated Shampoo reverses the GD ordering. Thus the optimizers change relative spectral progress rather than merely rescaling a common trajectory. Figure 2: Verification of the phase laws in Theorem 2 at depth L = 4 L=4 . (a) The birth exponent α b \alpha_{\mathrm{b}} separates Euclidean, normalized, history adapted, and curvature corrected dynamics. (b) The decay exponent α d \alpha_{\mathrm{d}} distinguishes finite extinction of Muon ( α d = q < 1 \alpha_{\mathrm{d}}\!=\!q\!<\!1 ) from the other optimizers. (c) The saturation coefficient β \beta reveals target dependent mode ordering. (a) Adam ϵ \epsilon controls the regime (b) Two phases of Shampoo (c) K-FAC λ KF > 0 \lambda_{\mathrm{KF}}\!>\!0 restores barrier Figure 3: Optimizer state parameters control the local birth regime. Adam’s stability parameter ϵ \epsilon shifts the GD-to-SignGD crossover; Shampoo damping delays the transition from p p to p − 1 p-1 ; and K-FAC damping restores the GD exponent below its curvature threshold.

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

matches.abstract_excerpt: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process.
