inspect:2610.20857.question: How was IDEA2PRIOR evaluated for paper retrieval and ranking? Identify the query set and ground-truth judgments, baseline access to the same corpus and evidence, Hit@5 accounting, cost and latency comparisons, and stated limitations.

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

passages.section: Appendix D Accounting, Reproducibility, and Artifact Scope
passages.text: The previous four-query Top 20 pilot is superseded as the primary retrieval evaluation by the present fixed-Top-5 comparison. Its variable-length baseline lists and asymmetric overlap denominators are not pooled with the new results. Historical attempts and the original manuscript remain preserved separately. The repository contains original browser response TXT files, selected Idea2Prior Top 5 outputs, Expert JSON, and prompt hashes for all three tiers. Timing uses the selected runs, including failed requests within them but excluding replaced whole-query attempts. Browser timings are operator-reported. Unknown usage remains null in source records. Gold data and supplied answer files are public for evaluation but must not be included in a new retrieval session. Consequently, this is a released benchmark, not a hidden test set. The revision performs no new model-based retrieval, paid API benchmark, or model-judge experiment. Numerical aggregation and document checks are local. Interface validation establishes software behavior, whereas the scientific conclusions derive from the stated historical cohorts. Public native-Gemini presets, new extension model trials, full MinerU processing, and a new full-report benchmark remain outside this evaluation. For a stronger follow-up study, freeze per-item prompts, source/configuration hashes, provider aliases, request budgets, and stop rules; isolate every browser session; report all attempts and final selections; record complete usage and tool charges; and adjudicate returned-paper relevance with independent raters. Because tiers share targets, comparisons should account for paired queries and repeated targets rather than treating all cases as independent observations.

passages.text: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49–59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79–86% accuracy, a significant 17–24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers .

Language agents that search the biomedical literature are quickly becoming a default component of scientific assistants: they formulate queries, read abstracts, and return verdicts with citations ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . The design space of such harnesses is large, but the empirical basis for choosing among designs is thin. Three questions arise for anyone building a literature agent for the life sciences: (i) Does giving a frontier model access to PubMed improve its verdicts over closed-book answering, or does parametric knowledge suffice? (ii) Is an agentic loop, in which the model writes and refines its own queries ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) , worth its additional cost over a fixed one-shot retrieval pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) ? (iii) When agents cite papers, are those citations faithful to what they actually read? We study these questions in a controlled setting: expert-written biomedical claim verification on SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) , using the live PubMed E-utilities API as the only tool. We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness : closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts. We run the same protocol with two backbones and decompose errors into retrieval failures (the gold paper was never seen) and reasoning failures (the gold paper was seen but the verdict was wrong).

(1) A small, fully reproducible harness-ablation protocol for literature agents built on a public benchmark and a public API (code and cached tool calls released). (2) An empirical comparison of four harnesses across two backbones, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired analyses. (3) A citation audit showing how closed-book models cite real but irrelevant papers, a failure mode that existence-based checks alone cannot catch.

Scientific claim verification. SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) introduced expert-written claims paired with evidence abstracts; subsequent systems such as MultiVerS ( Wadden et al., 2022 ) operate over a fixed corpus of about 5K abstracts. We instead place the model in the open-world setting it would face in deployment, searching all of PubMed. Retrieval-augmented and agentic biomedical QA. MedRAG ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) benchmarks retrieval-augmented generation for medical QA, GeneGPT ( Jin et al., 2024 ) teaches LLMs to call NCBI APIs, and PaperQA/PaperQA2 ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ) build full literature agents. LAB-Bench ( Laurent et al., 2024 ) evaluates biology-research capabilities including literature tasks. These works typically evaluate full systems; our aim is a minimal, controlled ablation of the harness itself. Citation fabrication. LLMs are known to fabricate bibliographic references ( Walters and Wilder, 2023 ) . We extend this analysis to PubMed IDs and distinguish non-existent citations from existing but irrelevant ones.

Implications for harness design. (1) Query formulation appears to be where the model adds the most value in a literature agent: letting the LLM reformulate the query triples recall of the right paper and gives the best verdicts on both backbones, whereas passing the claim straight to the search engine does not help. (2) The largest remaining headroom lies in retrieval, as the 17–24 point gap to the oracle shows, so iterative search that is actually used (F3), citation chasing, and domain retrievers are more promising than stronger verdict prompting. (3) Citations from ungrounded generation should never be surfaced, even when the IDs resolve: validating that a PMID exists is not sufficient, and relevance must be checked against the retrieved text. Limitations. This is a pilot study. N = 100 N{=}100 claims per condition gives wide confidence intervals, and none of the accuracy differences between realistic harnesses is significant. Both backbones are small, efficient models from a single provider, chosen for their low latency and cost, so results may differ for larger or open-weight models. SciFact labels are defined with respect to specific cited abstracts, whereas our harnesses search all of PubMed as of 2026. Some “errors” may therefore reflect newer or different evidence, and title-matched gold recall is a lower bound on useful retrieval. Relevance judgments come from a single LLM judge, validated only on 50 controls. We plan to scale to the full dev set, add open-weight and biomedical-specialist backbones, and study budget-forcing strategies for agentic search.

Reproducibility. Code, prompts, all raw model outputs, and the cached PubMed responses are available at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers . The released cache reproduces every reported number without API access.

Each arrow is a direction in the input activation space of a linear layer 𝑾 {\bm{W}} : its length is the spectral energy it carries, its orientation how much the network output depends on it (horizontal right: most), and faded arrows are removed. Activation-based low-rank compression (top) keeps the highest-energy directions, even when the output barely depends on them (red), and can discard functional ones (blue). LSP (bottom) learns the projector 𝑷 {\bm{P}} against the network output, removing the directions the output is least sensitive to, whatever their energy.

We propose Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which does exactly this: every projector is learned against a global objective, by default the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution, or alternatively the model’s original training objective, a variant we denote LSP T . Our contributions are: (1) Learned subspace projections. Layers that read the same activations (Q/K/V, gate/up) form a tied group and share one projector; we optimize all projectors jointly across the network with the pretrained weights frozen. An activation-space parameterization with fused QR orthonormalization keeps this tractable at billion-parameter scale. (2) Whitened initialization and measured-KL allocation. Each projector is initialized from a whitened truncation, recast as an orthogonal projector and extended to tied groups. To decide how many directions each layer or tied group removes, we apply each projector in isolation, measure the KL divergence it induces on the model output, and allocate the budget by KL cost per saved parameter. The model at initialization, which we call NoLSP, serves as a control that isolates the effect of learning. (3) Efficient low-rank inference. After training, the projectors merge into plain low-rank factors, so the deployed model contains no LSP-specific operations. At the same compression ratio it requires the same FLOPs per token as other factorizations, yet the input factor shared by each tied group speeds up small-batch decoding and, in a latent-cache deployment, stores one narrow latent per group where untied factorizations store two (one each for keys and values), shrinking the KV cache. Because LSP applies to any linear layer, the same recipe transfers across Transformer models without architecture-specific surgery. LSP outperforms pruning

or keys and values), shrinking the KV cache. Because LSP applies to any linear layer, the same recipe transfers across Transformer models without architecture-specific surgery. LSP outperforms pruning and SVD baselines by a margin that grows with the compression ratio, and on ViT it degrades least among the compared methods when calibration and evaluation distributions differ.

Setup. For language models we compress OPT-125M/1.3B ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) , Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-2-7B ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) . We report WikiText-2 ( Merity et al., 2016 ) test perplexity, calibrating as SliceGPT does on 1024 sequences of 2048 tokens from the training split, and zero-shot accuracy on six benchmarks with the calibration data given in Section 3.1 . Early stopping and every tuned setting are selected on held-out validation splits. On Qwen3-4B, whose grouped-query K and V are a quarter of Q’s width, K and V share an output-side projector and Q is projected alone; every other model ties Q/K/V on the input side ( Appendix B ). For vision we compress a ViT-B/16 ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) fine-tuned on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) and report source accuracy and linear-probe transfer. A compression ratio is the fraction of the parameters of the linear layers (no embeddings, no head) that is removed. All baselines run from their official code with the same calibration data and precision as LSP; SVD baselines are evaluated in factorized form, with tunable settings swept around the official optima ( Appendix B ).

Baselines. Activation- and reconstruction-based baselines , constructed from activation statistics or reconstruction criteria: SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , SVD-LLM (W) ( Wang et al., 2025d ) , whose whitening minimizes the layer-wise reconstruction error, and Swift-SVD ( Qi et al., 2026 ) , which reaches the same per-layer optimum from the output covariance and adds a per-matrix rank allocation. Loss-aware baselines use gradients of the loss: LLM-Surgeon ( van der Ouderaa et al., 2024 ) , through a Kronecker-factored curvature model, and Dobi-SVD ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , which learns only the per-matrix truncation rank within a closed-form basis, run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match. SVD-LLM is reported also with its LoRA recovery fine-tuning. On vision we compare with SliceGPT, SVD-LLM (W), FLAR-SVD ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) , and PELA ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . The last two are proposed on vision models, with PELA retraining all parameters by distilling every block’s output features from the dense model. NoLSP is the non-trained version of LSP, controlling for the learning stage at fixed initialization, ranks and ties.

Baselines. All baselines are using the same calibration budget of 1024 1024 sequences of 2048 2048 tokens, run with bf16 weights and compression arithmetic in fp32 or fp64 (following LSP), and, for the SVD methods, are evaluated in factorized form. Where a baseline exposes a tuning knob we sweep it around the published value and keep the best per model and ratio: SVD-LLM’s recovery learning rate against its single published one, Dobi-SVD’s γ \gamma learning rate around the released default, Swift-SVD’s allocation α \alpha over its own eleven-point grid, and ASVD’s α \alpha . Dobi-SVD is run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match; Swift-SVD’s OPT rows are bias-corrected; SVD-LLM’s recovery stage is LoRA of rank 8 8 on the calibration corpus of the table it appears in. Notice that LSP keeps original weights frozen, and learns to compress their subspace, which means it does not move from the original subspace but only projects. SVD-LLM-v2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) and MoDeGPT ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , though relevant, could not be reported as no official implementation has been released. The ViT ports of SVD-LLM (W) and SliceGPT are adapted from the official released implementation, while FLAR-SVD and PELA come from their official implementation. PELA, specifically, re-trains all the network’s weights with the objective to copy the dense model’s intermediate features, which acts as a recovery fine-tuning stage. Evaluation. Perplexity follows the SparseGPT and SliceGPT convention: the test split is joined, tokenized once and cut into non-overlapping 2048 2048 -token windows. Zero-shot accuracy is measured with the EleutherAI harness ( Gao et al., 2024a ) at zero shots on the merged model, and we report plain accuracy.

Modern transformers pair impressive capabilities with substantial memory and compute demands. Low-rank weight factorization reduces both while keeping the matrices dense, and thus efficient on standard hardware. Existing methods, however, choose the subspace to remove from each weight matrix with local closed-form criteria: activation energy, layer-wise reconstruction error, or a quadratic approximation of the loss. These criteria ignore how errors propagate through the network, so at high compression the errors compound with depth and performance collapses. We introduce Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which instead learns the subspaces to discard end-to-end. Each linear layer, or tied group of layers that read the same activations, is assigned an orthogonal projector. All projectors are optimized jointly against a global objective—the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution or the model’s original training loss—while the pretrained weights remain frozen. Projectors are initialized from a whitened SVD truncation, and ranks are allocated by the output KL each projector induces per parameter saved. After training, the projectors merge into standard low-rank factors, with each tied group sharing one factor. In attention, this also lets the model cache one narrow latent in place of full keys and values. Across LLMs (OPT-125M/1.3B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-2-7B) and ViT-B/16, LSP outperforms baselines, and its advantage widens as compression increases. Loss-aware baselines use gradients of the loss: LLM-Surgeon ( van der Ouderaa et al., 2024 ) , through a Kronecker-factored curvature model, and Dobi-SVD ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , which learns only the per-matrix truncation rank within a closed-form basis, run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match. SVD-LLM is reported also with its LoRA recovery fine-tuning. On vision we compare with SliceGPT, SVD-LLM (W), FLAR-SVD ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) , and PELA ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . The last two are proposed on vision models, with PELA retraining all parameters by distilling every block’s output features from the dense model. NoLSP is the non-trained version of LSP, controlling for the learning stage at fixed initialization, ranks and ties.

Baselines. All baselines are using the same calibration budget of 1024 1024 sequences of 2048 2048 tokens, run with bf16 weights and compression arithmetic in fp32 or fp64 (following LSP), and, for the SVD methods, are evaluated in factorized form. Where a baseline exposes a tuning knob we sweep it around the published value and keep the best per model and ratio: SVD-LLM’s recovery learning rate against its single published one, Dobi-SVD’s γ \gamma learning rate around the released default, Swift-SVD’s allocation α \alpha over its own eleven-point grid, and ASVD’s α \alpha . Dobi-SVD is run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match; Swift-SVD’s OPT rows are bias-corrected; SVD-LLM’s recovery stage is LoRA of rank 8 8 on the calibration corpus of the table it appears in. Notice that LSP keeps original weights frozen, and learns to compress their subspace, which means it does not move from the original subspace but only projects. SVD-LLM-v2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) and MoDeGPT ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , though relevant, could not be reported as no official implementation has been released. The ViT ports of SVD-LLM (W) and SliceGPT are adapted from the official released implementation, while FLAR-SVD and PELA come from their official implementation. PELA, specifically, re-trains all the network’s weights with the objective to copy the dense model’s intermediate features, which acts as a recovery fine-tuning stage. Evaluation. Perplexity follows the SparseGPT and SliceGPT convention: the test split is joined, tokenized once and cut into non-overlapping 2048 2048 -token windows. Zero-shot accuracy is measured with the EleutherAI harness ( Gao et al., 2024a ) at zero shots on the merged model, and we report plain accuracy.

Modern transformers pair impressive capabilities with substantial memory and compute demands. Low-rank weight factorization reduces both while keeping the matrices dense, and thus efficient on standard hardware. Existing methods, however, choose the subspace to remove from each weight matrix with local closed-form criteria: activation energy, layer-wise reconstruction error, or a quadratic approximation of the loss. These criteria ignore how errors propagate through the network, so at high compression the errors compound with depth and performance collapses. We introduce Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which instead learns the subspaces to discard end-to-end. Each linear layer, or tied group of layers that read the same activations, is assigned an orthogonal projector. All projectors are optimized jointly against a global objective—the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution or the model’s original training loss—while the pretrained weights remain frozen. Projectors are initialized from a whitened SVD truncation, and ranks are allocated by the output KL each projector induces per parameter saved. After training, the projectors merge into standard low-rank factors, with each tied group sharing one factor. In attention, this also lets the model cache one narrow latent in place of full keys and values. Across LLMs (OPT-125M/1.3B, Qwen3-4B, Llama-2-7B) and ViT-B/16, LSP outperforms baselines, and its advantage widens as compression increases. pending.reason: The inspected papers support ten selections across spectral training, compression, LoRA, memory-efficient optimization, and digest-agent retrieval. Uncertainty remains about independent replication and code reproducibility, but further available actions are unlikely to change this selection.

selections.summary: Spectral weight decay uses a decoupled nuclear-norm update to lower effective rank. In a 500M-parameter LLaMA experiment, it reports 1.89× compression and 1.18× inference speedup at a 4% distortion budget, versus 1.14× and 1.01× with standard weight decay.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses whether training improves low-rank compressibility while preserving validation quality, as well as robustness to label noise.

evidence.quote: Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss.

At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay.

selections.summary: ORCA applies soft orthogonality regularization early in LLM training, then removes it. The authors report lower final validation loss than Muon across several architectures and a matched-target LLaMA-1.3B run using 40% fewer tokens.
selections.relevance: Tests how the timing of spectral regularization affects rank and training quality.

evidence.quote: During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty
Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain.

selections.summary: Learnable Subspace Projections optimizes compression subspaces against a network-level objective while freezing pretrained weights. At 70% linear-layer parameter compression, its Llama-2-7B WikiText-2 perplexity is 10.9 versus 13.3 for SVD-LLM in the reported table.
selections.relevance: Provides a strong post-training low-rank compression comparator, with explicit baseline and calibration controls.

evidence.quote: NoLSP is the non-trained version of LSP, controlling for the learning stage at fixed initialization, ranks and ties.

selections.summary: PMRC retains optimizer states in a gradient subspace and corrects updates with the orthogonal residual. At 1.3B parameters, reported validation loss is 2.570, below AdamW and the tested memory-efficient baselines, but above full Muon’s 2.495; peak allocated memory is 53.44 GiB versus AdamW’s 57.77 GiB.
selections.relevance: Directly informs low-rank-gradient pretraining and the distinction between memory savings and best attainable quality.

selections.relevance: Gives measured quality, memory, and throughput tradeoffs for subspace optimization, albeit specifically under QAT.

selections.summary: Monarch-Muon applies Muon to structured factors. At a 6.9B dense reference size, its reported peak memory is 52.94 GB versus dense Muon’s 68.87 GB, and the authors report a 45% shorter full training step. Fixed-structure comparisons report lower validation loss than Monarch-AdamW.
selections.relevance: Connects parameterization, spectral optimization, model quality, training memory, and wall-clock cost at scale.

evidence.quote: Holding the Monarch factorization fixed isolates the effect of the optimizer.
At 6.89B, Monarch–Muon reduces the full-step time by 45% and peak memory by 23% relative to dense Muon.

selections.summary: A LoRA-specific Riemannian metric preconditions factor updates to better approximate full fine-tuning at the weight level. On LLaMA2-7B commonsense reasoning, reported average accuracy across eight tasks is 82.34% versus 81.68% for standard AdamW LoRA and 81.97% for conventional preconditioning.
selections.relevance: Addresses LoRA factorization geometry with a directly relevant language-model fine-tuning comparison.

evidence.quote: For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query, key, and value projections of the attention layers and the up and down projections of the feed-forward layers.

selections.summary: In a balanced, aligned matrix-factorization model, the paper derives how GD, SignGD, ideal Muon, cumulative Shampoo, and a K-FAC model differ in singular-mode birth, saturation, and decay. These are model-specific phase laws, not demonstrated LLM-training results.
selections.relevance: Offers a framework for studying how optimizer geometry changes spectral bias and effective rank.

evidence.quote: Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC.
Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior.

selections.summary: Idea2Prior combines identity checks, abstract assessment, citation expansion, and bounded PDF evidence for auditable paper ranking. Its historical 30-case evaluation reports 53.3% Hit@5, with a HARD-tier exception and longer latency than the compared browser systems.
selections.relevance: Directly informs evidence-grounded retrieval and ranking in a research-digest agent.

evidence.quote: It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking.
In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency.

selections.summary: A controlled SciFact harness ablation compares closed-book, single-query, ReAct-style search, and gold-abstract conditions while holding backbone and output format fixed. Agent-written queries improve gold-paper recall, but accuracy differences among realistic harnesses are not significant in this 100-claim-per-condition pilot.
selections.relevance: Provides concrete harness-design and citation-grounding lessons for a digest agent without establishing that the same effects transfer to arXiv digests.

evidence.quote: We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness : closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts.
N = 100 N{=}100 claims per condition gives wide confidence intervals, and none of the accuracy differences between realistic harnesses is significant.
validating that a PMID exists is not sufficient, and relevance must be checked against the retrieved text.

limitations: Results are reported by the papers’ authors; independent replication was not assessed.
Repository availability and runnable reproducibility were not verified.

Several results are setting-specific: ResQAdam targets QAT, the matrix-factorization phase laws assume balance and alignment, and the agent studies evaluate tasks other than research-digest selection.
X analysis was disabled, so no attention or popularity claims are made.

passages.text: To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

The main experiments use Adam-family optimizers. Conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay is routinely used across optimizer families, so we also examine whether spectral weight decay transfers beyond Adam. Its decoupled correction can be applied to the candidate weights produced by any optimizer, but the resulting loss and rank dynamics depend on the optimizer. Figure 6 : Optimizer-dependent loss and rank dynamics. The top row shows validation loss, and the bottom row shows mean effective rank. The columns compare ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with coefficient 0.1 0.1 across optimizers, spectral regularization with Muon, and spectral regularization with Lion. Colors match between the loss and rank panels. Figure 6 (a,d) compares optimizers with the same ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay coefficient of 0.1 0.1 . Muon [ Jordan et al., 2024 ] and SOAP [ Vyas et al., 2024 ] produce higher effective ranks than the other optimizers, whose final ranks cluster in a narrow range. This suggests that their optimization dynamics may oppose the spectral concentration encouraged by spectral weight decay. The Muon sweep in Figure 6 (b,e) shows that substantial rank reduction comes with a steep validation-loss increase, limiting the practical appeal of this combination. By contrast, Lion exhibits a more favorable trade-off between loss and rank in Figure 6 (c,f), qualitatively similar to Adam.

The required regularization scale also varies across optimizers. A mean effective rank of about 300 300 requires λ = 0.8 \lambda=0.8 for Adam, λ = 0.4 \lambda=0.4 for Muon, and λ = 4 \lambda=4 for Lion. Although the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} baselines use a common coefficient, spectral weight decay requires optimizer-specific calibration for the desired rank and validation-loss budget. The strong training results reported for Muon motivate adapting the techniques studied here to Muon and related matrix-aware optimizers. Understanding how to combine their optimization benefits with effective spectral regularization remains a direction for future work.

We introduced spectral weight decay by replacing the squared Frobenius penalty of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with the nuclear norm. Its decoupled post-step correction shrinks the spectrum of the updated weights additively, with a stronger relative effect on smaller singular values. The connection to approximate proximal descent supports this choice of update order. Our analysis also shows that pre- and post-step spectral updates can differ more substantially than their ℓ 2 \ell_{2} counterparts near rank deficiency. Across 124 124 M to 500 500 M LLaMA models trained with Adam-family optimizers, the resulting low-effective-rank structure improves post-training compression under matched validation-loss budgets. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, we obtain 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. The benefits extend beyond compression. Under fixed-horizon training with noisy labels, spectral regularization reduces memorization and improves clean-test accuracy on image and text classification tasks. These observations are consistent with the view that concentrating the weight spectrum limits the capacity available to fit corrupted labels. The benefits depend on when and how spectral regularization is applied. Short fine-tuning from a conventional-weight-decay checkpoint incurs a larger loss penalty for rank reduction than regularization during pretraining. Optimizer choice also matters: Adam and Lion exhibit a favorable trade-off between loss and rank, whereas the Muon runs show a steeper loss increase as rank decreases. Adapting spectral regularization to matrix-aware optimizers and reducing the cost of preparing existing checkpoints for low-rank compression remain open problems.

2610.23571:e233241fd1d35a0e8c91db03df3cb.question: For the 1B LLaMA-style FineWeb experiment, what are the matched Muon baselines, training and MLP channel-pruning budgets, validation-loss or downstream-quality results, and measured training overhead for BMuon?

passages.text: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon’s optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon’s spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning. Code: https://github.com/RidaAssalouh/BMuon † † shortheadings: BMuon / Assalouh et al.

Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.

To summarize, our main contributions are: • We introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which incorporates a single global hidden-channel budget into Muon’s spectral update geometry, while coupling the matrix slices that define each MLP channel. • We characterize the induced norm family Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} and its relation to Muon and structured sparse geometries in Section 2 . In the linear factorization setting of Section 3 , we show that for a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost is also attained by redundant-width factorizations. • We derive a practical minorization–maximization surrogate for the global allocation problem, yielding a tractable allocation update in Section 4 . • In Section 5 , we show across CIFAR-100, ImageNet-1K, and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model that BMuon improves structured MLP-channel compressibility relative to Muon. In the vision experiments, the learned allocations also provide effective pruning scores and identify non-uniform MLP architectures that outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch.

The BMuon construction on MLP hidden channels extends naturally to gated MLPs such as SwiGLU, as used in LLaMA-style models. The same allocation acts on the rows of the gate and up projections and on the columns of the down projection; see Appendix B.2 for details. Figure 3 : Post-training MLP-channel pruning at language-model scale. Validation perplexity after global structured pruning of a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb. Mean ± \pm std. over three seeds. To test whether BMuon’s structured-compressibility advantage extends to large-scale language modeling, we train a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model on 13.1B FineWeb tokens over three seeds. BMuon uses α = 1 / 2 \alpha=1/2 and K = 0.2 ​ N K=0.2N . After training, we globally prune SwiGLU hidden channels without recovery, using weight magnitude and an activation-aware score combining root-mean-square activation and output-weight norm; for BMuon, we also rank channels by μ \mu . The pruning curves are shown in Figure 3 ; full details are given in Appendix E.5 . On the unpruned models, Muon achieves lower perplexity ( 10.92 10.92 versus 12.84 12.84 for BMuon), but its performance degrades rapidly under pruning. In contrast, BMuon preserves its unpruned performance up to 80 % 80\% pruning, reaching 12.86 12.86 with activation ranking and 12.85 12.85 with μ \mu ranking. BMuon substantially outperforms Muon when both use the same magnitude or activation criterion at moderate and high pruning levels, while μ \mu again provides an effective pruning score. Overall, BMuon trades some unpruned quality for substantially greater robustness to structured channel pruning.

Our LLaMA/FineWeb experiments are based on the LLaMA-1B setup of Muon+ ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) 1 1 1 https://github.com/K1seki221/MuonPlus . We adopt its architecture and training recipe, reducing only the number of Transformer blocks from 24 24 to 17 17 to obtain a 986,746,880 986{,}746{,}880 -parameter model; all other architectural hyperparameters are unchanged. The Muon+ codebase builds on Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) and the modded-nanogpt training framework 2 2 2 https://github.com/KellerJordan/modded-nanogpt . We retain its LLaMA-2 tokenizer and FineWeb preprocessing and sharding conventions, Muon parameter routing, auxiliary AdamW-style updates for non-Muon parameters, momentum/Nesterov convention, five-step Newton–Schulz polar approximation, matrix learning-rate shape/RMS scaling, warmup–cosine schedule, and BF16 training conventions. For our experiments, we integrate BMuon into the SwiGLU MLPs.

2610.06116:8c303342bcf03feb64a2ace598c92.question: Across the LLaMA, Qwen3, and MoE pretraining experiments, what matched Muon and Adam baselines, training-token budgets, final validation-loss results, and measured throughput or compute overhead support ORCA's gains?

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. The Qwen3 0.6B curves cover 50k optimizer steps (about 105B tokens), and the Qwen3 160M curves cover 25k optimizer steps (about 26B tokens). We observed router perturbations under a fixed global release point, so we release the orthogonal constraint layerwise: at 20 % 20\% of training in the first layer and at 60 % 60\% in the last layer, with release times linearly interpolated across layers. We use top- 4 4 routing with 64 64 experts in the MoE 0.8 0.8 B model ( 0.24 0.24 B active parameters) and 64 64 experts in the MoE 8 8 B model ( 1 1 B active parameters) ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

Early orthogonal shaping also benefits other base optimizers. We apply the same soft orthogonal shaping step ( 3.3 ) to Adam and SOAP on LLaMA 130M ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) . Shaping is active only during the first 25 % 25\% of training; the base optimizer then continues alone. For both optimizers, shaping temporarily raises validation loss while active, but the shaped runs overtake their baselines after its removal and finish lower. At 50k steps, it reduces Adam’s loss from 2.8824 2.8824 to 2.8435 2.8435 and SOAP’s from 2.8640 2.8640 to 2.8271 2.8271 , gains of 0.0389 0.0389 and 0.0369 0.0369 , respectively. These results show that the benefits of early orthogonal shaping extend beyond Muon to other base optimizers. passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} . This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation ( B , A ) ∼ ( B ​ G − 1 , A ​ G ⊤ ) (B,A)\sim(BG^{-1},AG^{\top}) for any invertible matrix G G because B ​ A ⊤ = B ​ G − 1 ​ ( A ​ G ⊤ ) ⊤ BA^{\top}=BG^{-1}(AG^{\top})^{\top} and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices ( B ​ G − 1 , A ​ G ⊤ ) (BG^{-1},AG^{\top}) for all G G are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. We theoretically show that LoRA with our preconditioning induced by this metric satisfies the following two properties at each iteration: (i) The weight update follows the direction closest to the gradient of full fine-tuning within the subspace of first-order weight changes allowed by the LoRA parameterization. (ii) The updated weight matrix is closer in Frobenius norm to that of full fine-tuning than the updated weight matrices of LoRA with conventional preconditioning and without preconditioning. These theoretical insights suggest that our preconditioning makes LoRA better approximate full fine-tuning, thereby

ight matrices of LoRA with conventional preconditioning and without preconditioning. These theoretical insights suggest that our preconditioning makes LoRA better approximate full fine-tuning, thereby leading to more efficient optimization. Experiments show the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning for LoRA on fine-tuning tasks with language and vision domains.

To validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning 5 for LoRA, we conducted LoRA fine-tuning experiments on natural language generation, image classification, and commonsense reasoning tasks, following the existing LoRA studies [ 21 , 63 , 56 , 41 , 26 ] . All experiments were performed in PyTorch [ 42 ] on a single H100 GPU with 80 GB VRAM. We downloaded the pre-trained models using Hugging Face Transformers library [ 57 ] .

Following [ 26 , 41 , 16 ] , we conducted LoRA fine-tuning for the LLaMA2-7B [ 52 ] on the commonsense reasoning benchmark, which assesses the reasoning capabilities of the fine-tuned model across the eight datasets, such as BoolQ [ 8 ] , PIQA [ 5 ] , SIQA [ 48 ] , HellaS [ 62 ] , WinoG [ 47 ] , ARC-e [ 9 ] , ARC-c [ 9 ] , and OBQA [ 35 ] . In these datasets, we measured the top-1 test accuracy. For fair comparison, we first split a combined dataset of all train sets, i.e., Commonsense170K, into the train and validation sets, tuned the learning rate on the validation set, and then evaluated the fine-tuned model on the test set in each dataset. In this experiment, we tested the Adam methods with preconditioning. We tuned the learning rate over { 0.0001 , 0.0002 , … , 0.001 } \{0.0001,0.0002,\dots,0.001\} for each method on the validation set, similar to Sec. 7.3 . For all methods, we inserted the low-rank matrix B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} into the query, key, and value projections of the attention layers and the up and down projections of the feed-forward layers. We also fixed the rank to r = 32 r=32 , the scaling factor of B ​ A ⊤ BA^{\top} to 64 64 , the batch size to 16 16 , the weight decay to zero, the dropout to 0.05 0.05 , and the train epoch to 3 3 with a linear learning-rate schedule. Table 3 shows the results. We observed that our AdamW method achieves either the highest or second-highest top-1 test accuracy across datasets, leading to the highest average. These results validate the effectiveness of our preconditioning for LoRA on the commonsense reasoning task.

In this paper, we proposed a Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. This metric induces new preconditioning, and we theoretically showed that this preconditioning makes LoRA better approximates full fine-tuning compared with the conventional preconditioning and no preconditioning. Diverse experiments showed the effectiveness and efficiency of our preconditioning in the language and vision domains. This paper is the first to explore the possibility of tailoring a Riemannian metric to LoRA, paving the way for future followers.

2610.04249:46ab08cb23af2aec8780c6832e9a0.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results for GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC? Which predictions are tested empirically on neural networks or language models, against which optimizer baselines, and what limitations are stated?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. (a) GD (b) Muon (c) GD vs Muon: Birth and decay

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

The decay curves distinguish finite extinction under ideal Muon, exponential decay under undamped K-FAC, and the polynomial tails of GD and cumulative Shampoo. The saturation experiment further reveals optimizer-dependent mode ordering: GD and Adam converge faster for larger targets; undamped K-FAC is approximately target independent while Muon shows dependence; history-dominated Shampoo reverses the GD ordering. Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Analysis of Muon in matrix factorization.
passages.text: Kang et al. (2026) analyze spectral gradient flow in a simplified LoRA factorization setting, proving approximately equal spectral growth rates and convergence results under stated conditions. Dragutinović and Ranganath (2026) derive dynamics for simplified Muon in deep linear networks and linear attention and investigate how avoiding slow sequential learning changes simplicity bias. Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. They also study alignment in simplified settings. These results already establish much of the ideal polar growth baseline. Our treatment places it alongside memory dependent adaptive flows and damped curvature flows, with separate statements for birth, saturation, and zero target decay. Parviz et al. (2026) report controlled optimizer comparisons showing that Muon’s relative performance in factorization depends on the problem and hyperparameter tuning. This motivates separating exact polar flow predictions from practical implementation effects and comparing recovery at a common training fit.

This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs.
