Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

passages.section: Appendix D Accounting, Reproducibility, and Artifact Scope
passages.text: The previous four-query Top 20 pilot is superseded as the primary retrieval evaluation by the present fixed-Top-5 comparison. Its variable-length baseline lists and asymmetric overlap denominators are not pooled with the new results. Historical attempts and the original manuscript remain preserved separately. The repository contains original browser response TXT files, selected Idea2Prior Top 5 outputs, Expert JSON, and prompt hashes for all three tiers. Timing uses the selected runs, including failed requests within them but excluding replaced whole-query attempts. Browser timings are operator-reported. Unknown usage remains null in source records. Gold data and supplied answer files are public for evaluation but must not be included in a new retrieval session. Consequently, this is a released benchmark, not a hidden test set. The revision performs no new model-based retrieval, paid API benchmark, or model-judge experiment. Numerical aggregation and document checks are local. Interface validation establishes software behavior, whereas the scientific conclusions derive from the stated historical cohorts. Public native-Gemini presets, new extension model trials, full MinerU processing, and a new full-report benchmark remain outside this evaluation. For a stronger follow-up study, freeze per-item prompts, source/configuration hashes, provider aliases, request budgets, and stop rules; isolate every browser session; report all attempts and final selections; record complete usage and tool charges; and adjudicate returned-paper relevance with independent raters. Because tiers share targets, comparisons should account for paired queries and repeated targets rather than treating all cases as independent observations.

2610.29812:736d4fd47c91ee950c4ddab647b3c.question: In the SciFact harness ablation, how were the four retrieval strategies and two backbones controlled, what were gold-paper recall and verdict accuracy with uncertainty estimates, and what limitations affect transfer to a research-digest agent?

passages.text: Literature-searching language agents are becoming a standard component of scientific assistants for the life sciences, yet there is little controlled evidence on which parts of their harness matter. We run a controlled ablation on biomedical claim verification (SciFact) with the live PubMed API as the only tool. Holding the backbone and output format fixed, we compare four harnesses: closed-book answering, single-shot retrieval using the claim as the query, a ReAct-style agent that writes its own PubMed queries, and an oracle given the gold abstracts, each with two efficient frontier backbones. Naive single-shot retrieval finds the gold paper for only 6% of claims and turns overconfident errors into abstentions without improving accuracy. Letting the model formulate its own queries triples gold recall and yields the best verdicts (62% accuracy vs. 49–59% for the other realistic harnesses), although these differences are not significant at our sample size and agents use fewer than half of their search budget. With gold abstracts, the same models reach 79–86% accuracy, a significant 17–24 point gap showing that retrieval, not reasoning, is the main bottleneck. Finally, a citation audit shows that closed-book models cite PubMed IDs that almost always exist (327/335) but are almost never relevant: a cross-family LLM judge rates only 3 of 327 existing citations as relevant to the claim, versus 67% for citations produced by the search agent. Existence checks are therefore insufficient safeguards for scientific agents. We release code, prompts, and all cached tool calls at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers .

Language agents that search the biomedical literature are quickly becoming a default component of scientific assistants: they formulate queries, read abstracts, and return verdicts with citations ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ; Jin et al., 2024 ) . The design space of such harnesses is large, but the empirical basis for choosing among designs is thin. Three questions arise for anyone building a literature agent for the life sciences: (i) Does giving a frontier model access to PubMed improve its verdicts over closed-book answering, or does parametric knowledge suffice? (ii) Is an agentic loop, in which the model writes and refines its own queries ( Yao et al., 2023 ; Nakano et al., 2021 ) , worth its additional cost over a fixed one-shot retrieval pipeline ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) ? (iii) When agents cite papers, are those citations faithful to what they actually read? We study these questions in a controlled setting: expert-written biomedical claim verification on SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) , using the live PubMed E-utilities API as the only tool. We hold the backbone model, prompt format, and output schema fixed and vary only the harness : closed-book, single-shot retrieval, a ReAct-style multi-query agent, and an oracle that receives the gold abstracts. We run the same protocol with two backbones and decompose errors into retrieval failures (the gold paper was never seen) and reasoning failures (the gold paper was seen but the verdict was wrong).

(1) A small, fully reproducible harness-ablation protocol for literature agents built on a public benchmark and a public API (code and cached tool calls released). (2) An empirical comparison of four harnesses across two backbones, with bootstrap confidence intervals and paired analyses. (3) A citation audit showing how closed-book models cite real but irrelevant papers, a failure mode that existence-based checks alone cannot catch.

Scientific claim verification. SciFact ( Wadden et al., 2020 ) introduced expert-written claims paired with evidence abstracts; subsequent systems such as MultiVerS ( Wadden et al., 2022 ) operate over a fixed corpus of about 5K abstracts. We instead place the model in the open-world setting it would face in deployment, searching all of PubMed. Retrieval-augmented and agentic biomedical QA. MedRAG ( Xiong et al., 2024 ) benchmarks retrieval-augmented generation for medical QA, GeneGPT ( Jin et al., 2024 ) teaches LLMs to call NCBI APIs, and PaperQA/PaperQA2 ( Lála et al., 2023 ; Skarlinski et al., 2024 ) build full literature agents. LAB-Bench ( Laurent et al., 2024 ) evaluates biology-research capabilities including literature tasks. These works typically evaluate full systems; our aim is a minimal, controlled ablation of the harness itself. Citation fabrication. LLMs are known to fabricate bibliographic references ( Walters and Wilder, 2023 ) . We extend this analysis to PubMed IDs and distinguish non-existent citations from existing but irrelevant ones.

Implications for harness design. (1) Query formulation appears to be where the model adds the most value in a literature agent: letting the LLM reformulate the query triples recall of the right paper and gives the best verdicts on both backbones, whereas passing the claim straight to the search engine does not help. (2) The largest remaining headroom lies in retrieval, as the 17–24 point gap to the oracle shows, so iterative search that is actually used (F3), citation chasing, and domain retrievers are more promising than stronger verdict prompting. (3) Citations from ungrounded generation should never be surfaced, even when the IDs resolve: validating that a PMID exists is not sufficient, and relevance must be checked against the retrieved text. Limitations. This is a pilot study. N = 100 N{=}100 claims per condition gives wide confidence intervals, and none of the accuracy differences between realistic harnesses is significant. Both backbones are small, efficient models from a single provider, chosen for their low latency and cost, so results may differ for larger or open-weight models. SciFact labels are defined with respect to specific cited abstracts, whereas our harnesses search all of PubMed as of 2026. Some “errors” may therefore reflect newer or different evidence, and title-matched gold recall is a lower bound on useful retrieval. Relevance judgments come from a single LLM judge, validated only on 50 controls. We plan to scale to the full dev set, add open-weight and biomedical-specialist backbones, and study budget-forcing strategies for agentic search.

Reproducibility. Code, prompts, all raw model outputs, and the cached PubMed responses are available at https://github.com/saqlain2204/real-pmids-wrong-papers . The released cache reproduces every reported number without API access.

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

2609.40127:fed96587f11204f5a229c2f1150dc.question: For LSP low-rank compression experiments, what models and compression ratios are tested, which SVD-based and learned-subspace baselines share the same evaluation and recovery budget, and what measured validation-loss, downstream-quality, memory, or inference-speed results show whether quality is preserved?

passages.text: Figure 1: Spectral energy is not function. Each arrow is a direction in the input activation space of a linear layer 𝑾 {\bm{W}} : its length is the spectral energy it carries, its orientation how much the network output depends on it (horizontal right: most), and faded arrows are removed. Activation-based low-rank compression (top) keeps the highest-energy directions, even when the output barely depends on them (red), and can discard functional ones (blue). LSP (bottom) learns the projector 𝑷 {\bm{P}} against the network output, removing the directions the output is least sensitive to, whatever their energy.

We propose Learnable Subspace Projections (LSP), which does exactly this: every projector is learned against a global objective, by default the KL divergence to the dense model’s output distribution, or alternatively the model’s original training objective, a variant we denote LSP T . Our contributions are: (1) Learned subspace projections. Layers that read the same activations (Q/K/V, gate/up) form a tied group and share one projector; we optimize all projectors jointly across the network with the pretrained weights frozen. An activation-space parameterization with fused QR orthonormalization keeps this tractable at billion-parameter scale. (2) Whitened initialization and measured-KL allocation. Each projector is initialized from a whitened truncation, recast as an orthogonal projector and extended to tied groups. To decide how many directions each layer or tied group removes, we apply each projector in isolation, measure the KL divergence it induces on the model output, and allocate the budget by KL cost per saved parameter. The model at initialization, which we call NoLSP, serves as a control that isolates the effect of learning. (3) Efficient low-rank inference. After training, the projectors merge into plain low-rank factors, so the deployed model contains no LSP-specific operations. At the same compression ratio it requires the same FLOPs per token as other factorizations, yet the input factor shared by each tied group speeds up small-batch decoding and, in a latent-cache deployment, stores one narrow latent per group where untied factorizations store two (one each for keys and values), shrinking the KV cache. Because LSP applies to any linear layer, the same recipe transfers across Transformer models without architecture-specific surgery. LSP outperforms pruning

LSP outperforms pruning and SVD baselines by a margin that grows with the compression ratio, and on ViT it degrades least among the compared methods when calibration and evaluation distributions differ.

Setup. For language models we compress OPT-125M/1.3B ( Zhang et al., 2022 ) , Qwen3-4B ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-2-7B ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) . We report WikiText-2 ( Merity et al., 2016 ) test perplexity, calibrating as SliceGPT does on 1024 sequences of 2048 tokens from the training split, and zero-shot accuracy on six benchmarks with the calibration data given in Section 3.1 . Early stopping and every tuned setting are selected on held-out validation splits. On Qwen3-4B, whose grouped-query K and V are a quarter of Q’s width, K and V share an output-side projector and Q is projected alone; every other model ties Q/K/V on the input side ( Appendix B ). For vision we compress a ViT-B/16 ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) fine-tuned on CIFAR-100 ( Krizhevsky, 2009 ) and report source accuracy and linear-probe transfer. A compression ratio is the fraction of the parameters of the linear layers (no embeddings, no head) that is removed. All baselines run from their official code with the same calibration data and precision as LSP; SVD baselines are evaluated in factorized form, with tunable settings swept around the official optima ( Appendix B ).

Baselines. Activation- and reconstruction-based baselines , constructed from activation statistics or reconstruction criteria: SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , ASVD ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , SVD-LLM (W) ( Wang et al., 2025d ) , whose whitening minimizes the layer-wise reconstruction error, and Swift-SVD ( Qi et al., 2026 ) , which reaches the same per-layer optimum from the output covariance and adds a per-matrix rank allocation. Loss-aware baselines use gradients of the loss: LLM-Surgeon ( van der Ouderaa et al., 2024 ) , through a Kronecker-factored curvature model, and Dobi-SVD ( Wang et al., 2025b ) , which learns only the per-matrix truncation rank within a closed-form basis, run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match. SVD-LLM is reported also with its LoRA recovery fine-tuning. On vision we compare with SliceGPT, SVD-LLM (W), FLAR-SVD ( Thoma et al., 2025 ) , and PELA ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . The last two are proposed on vision models, with PELA retraining all parameters by distilling every block’s output features from the dense model. NoLSP is the non-trained version of LSP, controlling for the learning stage at fixed initialization, ranks and ties.

Baselines. All baselines are using the same calibration budget of 1024 1024 sequences of 2048 2048 tokens, run with bf16 weights and compression arithmetic in fp32 or fp64 (following LSP), and, for the SVD methods, are evaluated in factorized form. Where a baseline exposes a tuning knob we sweep it around the published value and keep the best per model and ratio: SVD-LLM’s recovery learning rate against its single published one, Dobi-SVD’s γ \gamma learning rate around the released default, Swift-SVD’s allocation α \alpha over its own eleven-point grid, and ASVD’s α \alpha . Dobi-SVD is run without its quantization step so that parameter counts match; Swift-SVD’s OPT rows are bias-corrected; SVD-LLM’s recovery stage is LoRA of rank 8 8 on the calibration corpus of the table it appears in. Notice that LSP keeps original weights frozen, and learns to compress their subspace, which means it does not move from the original subspace but only projects. SVD-LLM-v2 ( Wang et al., 2025c ) and MoDeGPT ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , though relevant, could not be reported as no official implementation has been released. The ViT ports of SVD-LLM (W) and SliceGPT are adapted from the official released implementation, while FLAR-SVD and PELA come from their official implementation. PELA, specifically, re-trains all the network’s weights with the objective to copy the dense model’s intermediate features, which acts as a recovery fine-tuning stage. Evaluation. Perplexity follows the SparseGPT and SliceGPT convention: the test split is joined, tokenized once and cut into non-overlapping 2048 2048 -token windows. Zero-shot accuracy is measured with the EleutherAI harness ( Gao et al., 2024a ) at zero shots on the merged model, and we report plain accuracy.

passages.text: Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

passages.text: Following the standard practical implementation of Muon, we retain the shape-dependent learning-rate scaling factor 0.2 ​ max ⁡ { m , n } 0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}} and weight decay with coefficient λ \lambda . These two components are inherited from Liu et al. (2025) . We set ρ = 4 \rho=4 and ϵ = 10 − 30 \epsilon=10^{-30} in our experiments. Second, periodic SVD computations in GaLore introduce time overhead when the projection basis is refreshed, particularly for high-dimensional matrices. To improve computational efficiency, we replace the exact SVD with a warm-started subspace approximation adapted from ARO ( Gong et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, given the matrix G ∈ ℝ m × n G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and the previous basis P prev ∈ ℝ m × r P^{\mathrm{prev}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} , we update the basis by P = QR ⁡ ( G ​ f RN ​ ( ( P prev ) ⊤ ​ G ) ⊤ ) , P=\operatorname{QR}\!\left(G\,f_{\mathrm{RN}}\!\left((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^{\top}G\right)^{\top}\right), where f RN ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{\mathrm{RN}}(\cdot) performs row normalization and QR ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{QR}(\cdot) returns an orthonormal basis. The corresponding singular values are estimated from the row norms of P ⊤ ​ G P^{\top}G . In our implementation, the QR operation is computed with SCQR ( Fukaya et al., 2020 ) . Setup. We train the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models on 2 2 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs, the 350 350 M model on 4 4 NVIDIA H20 GPUs, and the 1.3 1.3 B model on 8 8 NVIDIA H20 GPUs. The corresponding per-device batch sizes are 256 256 , 256 256 , 160 160 , and 160 160 , yielding global batch sizes of 512 512 , 512 512 , 640 640 , and 1280 1280 , respectively. The sequence length is 512 512 for the 60 60 M and 150 150 M models and 1024 1024 for the 350 350 M and 1.3 1.3 B models. For each model, the number of training steps approximately follows the Chinchilla scaling law ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) . For example, the 1.3 1.3 B model is trained for 20480 20480 steps, which corresponds to 20480 × 1024 × 1280 ≈ 26.84 20480\times 1024\times 1280\approx 26.84 billion training tokens, or approximately 20.6 20.6 tokens per parameter. We compare our multi-stage PMRC with AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) , Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) , the AdamW-based GaLore ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , GoLore ( He et al., 2025 ) and Fira ( Chen et al., 2025a ) , and the Muon-based GUM ( Pan et al., 2025a ) . For projection-based methods, we set the projection rank to r = 256 r=256 and the refresh interval to 100 100 . Since GUM randomly selects a subset of layers for full-rank updates, its memory cost depends on the number of full-rank layers s s . For a fair comparison, we choose s s according to the memory budget of PMRC, setting s = 6 s=6 and r = 128 r=128 for the 60 60 M, 150 150 M, and 350 350 M models, and s = 4 s=4 and r = 128 r=128 for the 1.3 1.3 B model. The peak allocated memory for the 1.3 1.3 B model is reported in Table 6 . The detailed setup, parameter settings and additional pretraining results are deferred to Appendix E.2.2 .

Results. Table 1 presents a comparison of the training and validation losses achieved by PMRC with those achieved by AdamW, Muon, GaLore, GoLore, Fira and GUM. As evidenced by the reported results, PMRC consistently achieves the lowest training and validation losses among memory-efficient methods. The improvement supports the effectiveness of residual correction in practical LLM pretraining. PMRC also requires less optimizer-state memory than AdamW while achieving lower losses at every scale. We further evaluate the pretrained models on seven downstream benchmarks, with complete results reported in Appendix E.2.2 , where PMRC achieves the highest average accuracy among memory-efficient methods.

Following the standard practical implementation of Muon, we retain the shape-dependent learning-rate scaling factor 0.2 ​ max ⁡ { m , n } 0.2\sqrt{\max\{m,n\}} and weight decay with coefficient λ \lambda . These two components are inherited from Liu et al. (2025) . We set ρ = 4 \rho=4 and ϵ = 10 − 30 \epsilon=10^{-30} in our experiments. Second, periodic SVD computations in GaLore introduce time overhead when the projection basis is refreshed, particularly for high-dimensional matrices. To improve computational efficiency, we replace the exact SVD with a warm-started subspace approximation adapted from ARO ( Gong et al., 2026 ) . Specifically, given the matrix G ∈ ℝ m × n G\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} and the previous basis P prev ∈ ℝ m × r P^{\mathrm{prev}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r} , we update the basis by P = QR ⁡ ( G ​ f RN ​ ( ( P prev ) ⊤ ​ G ) ⊤ ) , P=\operatorname{QR}\!\left(G\,f_{\mathrm{RN}}\!\left((P^{\mathrm{prev}})^{\top}G\right)^{\top}\right), where f RN ​ ( ⋅ ) f_{\mathrm{RN}}(\cdot) performs row normalization and QR ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \operatorname{QR}(\cdot) returns an orthonormal basis. The corresponding singular values are estimated from the row norms of P ⊤ ​ G P^{\top}G . In our implementation, the QR operation is computed with SCQR ( Fukaya et al., 2020 ) .
